result: Enzalutamide treatment sustains cortisol levels by impairing conversion to cortisone in cell lines and xenograft models, and cell growth recovers after sustained enzalutamide treatment.
evaluation: Claims C9, C10, and C13 are supported by experimental data showing that long-term (but not short-term) enzalutamide exposure retards cortisol inactivation in LAPC4 and VCaP cells (Figure 1B) and xenografts (Figure 1C), and that cell viability recovers with prolonged treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C). These findings establish the metabolic phenotype associated with enzalutamide resistance.

result: Enzalutamide treatment causes loss of 11β-HSD2 protein in AR-expressing prostate cancer cell lines and patient tissues, but not through transcriptional suppression, direct antagonism, or GR stimulation.
evaluation: Claims C14-C23 are well-supported by Western blot and immunofluorescence data from multiple cell lines (Figure 2A-D) and patient tissues (Figure 2E). The mechanism is shown to be post-transcriptional (C17-C18) and not due to direct enzyme inhibition (C19) or GR stimulation (C20). The clinical relevance is demonstrated in 9 of 11 patient samples (C21), with GR upregulation observed in a subset that also showed 11β-HSD2 loss (C22-C23).

result: Reinstatement of 11β-HSD2 expression reverses the metabolic phenotype of enzalutamide treatment and specifically affects GR-responsive genes.
evaluation: Claims C24 and C25 are supported by experimental data showing that both transient and stable 11β-HSD2 expression restore rapid cortisol inactivation (Figure 3A-B) and that the effects are specific to cortisol (not dexamethasone) and GR-responsive genes like PSA and KLF9 (Figure 3C). The specificity controls using PMEPA1 (AR-only regulated) strengthen the conclusion.

result: Forced 11β-HSD2 expression reverses enzalutamide resistance in xenograft models by depleting intratumoral glucocorticoids without affecting systemic levels.
evaluation: Claims C26-C32 are strongly supported by in vivo xenograft data showing that 11β-HSD2 expression significantly reduces tumor growth and prolongs progression-free survival in both LAPC4 and VCaP models treated with enzalutamide (Figure 4A-D), but has no effect on untreated tumors (C27). Mass spectrometry data confirm significant depletion of tumor corticosterone (C29-C30) without affecting serum levels (C31-C32), demonstrating tumor-specific metabolic effects.

result: AMFR physically interacts with 11β-HSD2, mediates its ubiquitination and degradation, and is required for the metabolic phenotype of enzalutamide resistance.
evaluation: Claims C33-C41 are supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments (C33, Figure 5A), ubiquitination assays (C34, Figure 5B), and functional studies showing that AMFR knockdown increases 11β-HSD2 protein (C37) but not transcript (C38), reverses the metabolic phenotype (C39), and that the effect requires 11β-HSD2 (C40-C41, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E). The mechanistic chain is well-established.

result: AMFR knockdown suppresses enzalutamide-resistant xenograft growth and prolongs progression-free survival by sustaining 11β-HSD2 expression.
evaluation: Claims C42 and C43 are supported by in vivo data showing that AMFR knockdown significantly reduces tumor growth and extends progression-free survival in enzalutamide-treated xenografts (Figure 5E-F), with confirmation that these tumors retain 11β-HSD2 expression (Figure 5G). This validates AMFR as a therapeutic target.

result: Erlin-2, but not AMFR, is consistently upregulated with enzalutamide treatment in cell lines and patient tissues.
evaluation: Claims C35 and C36 are supported by Western blot data showing inconsistent AMFR upregulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B) but consistent Erlin-2 upregulation in 8 of 11 patient tissues (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C). This suggests Erlin-2 may be the primary driver of enhanced ERAD activity rather than increased AMFR expression.

result: Enzalutamide suppresses LAPC4 cell viability and AR-regulated gene expression.
evaluation: Claims C11 and C12 are supported by cell viability assays (Figure 1D) and qPCR data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) showing that enzalutamide reduces cell viability and suppresses AR-regulated genes. These are expected effects that validate the experimental system.

result: Enzalutamide is an effective AR antagonist that prolongs survival in metastatic CRPC, but resistance inevitably develops.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C44, C45, and C46 are background claims supported by multiple citations to established literature. These provide the clinical context for the study but are not novel findings from this work.

result: Enzalutamide-induced GR upregulation permits re-expression of AR-responsive genes, but systemic GR blockade is not viable therapeutically.
evaluation: Claims C3, C4, and C5 are supported by citations to prior work establishing the rationale for this study. These claims provide important context for why a tumor-specific metabolic approach is needed but are not novel findings.

result: 11β-HSD2 converts cortisol to cortisone in humans and corticosterone to 11-dehydrocorticosterone in mice, and is localized to the endoplasmic reticulum.
evaluation: Claims C6, C7, C8, C48, C70, C71, and C74 are established biochemical facts supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A. These provide necessary background on glucocorticoid metabolism but are not novel findings.

result: The study demonstrates that AMFR-mediated loss of 11β-HSD2 sustains tumor cortisol levels to drive GR-dependent enzalutamide resistance, which can be reversed by restoring 11β-HSD2 or blocking AMFR.
evaluation: Claims C47, C49-C55 are summary statements of the main findings, supported by the comprehensive experimental data throughout the manuscript. These integrate the mechanistic findings (AMFR-mediated 11β-HSD2 degradation), metabolic consequences (sustained cortisol), and therapeutic implications (reversibility of resistance).

result: Local tumor metabolic regulation of glucocorticoid availability is a critical determinant of GR stimulation in addition to systemic glucocorticoid levels.
evaluation: Claims C56 and C57 represent key conceptual conclusions supported by the finding that tumor-specific 11β-HSD2 expression depletes intratumoral glucocorticoids without affecting systemic levels (C29-C32). This establishes a new paradigm for understanding GR signaling in cancer.

result: Glucocorticoid pharmacology in prostate cancer is complex, with differential susceptibility to 11β-HSD2 inactivation and potential relevance to baseline GR expression and abiraterone therapy.
evaluation: Claims C58-C63 are discussion points supported by citations to prior work. They contextualize the findings within existing clinical knowledge about glucocorticoid therapy in CRPC and suggest broader implications, but do not present new experimental data.

result: The findings suggest potential therapeutic strategies targeting AMFR or 11β-HSD2 to reverse enzalutamide resistance without systemic toxicity, though AMFR inhibition may have complex effects on androgen synthesis.
evaluation: Claims C64-C67 are speculative proposals for future therapeutic approaches. While C67 is supported by the in vivo AMFR knockdown data (Figure 5E-F), claims C64-C66 are explicitly presented as possibilities requiring further investigation. The therapeutic potential is plausible but not yet validated.

result: The mechanism of steroid receptor switching accompanied by altered local metabolic regulation may have broader relevance beyond prostate cancer.
evaluation: Claims C68 and C69 are speculative extensions of the findings to other disease contexts. While C68 is supported by citations about GR/AR in breast cancer, C69 is an inference that requires experimental validation in other systems.

result: AMFR is an E3 ubiquitin ligase in the ERAD pathway that regulates steroidogenic enzymes, and Erlin-2 enables AMFR-associated ERAD.
evaluation: Claims C72, C73, and C75 are supported by citations to prior work from the same laboratory and others. These establish the known functions of AMFR and Erlin-2 that provide the mechanistic basis for the current findings.

result: A model is proposed in which physical association between AMFR and 11β-HSD2 enables enzalutamide to promote 11β-HSD2 loss, resulting in sustained cortisol and GR stimulation.
evaluation: Claim C76 is a mechanistic model inferred from the experimental data in Figure 5. The physical association (C33), ubiquitination (C34), and functional consequences (C37-C43) collectively support this model, though the precise mechanism by which enzalutamide triggers this process remains to be fully elucidated.

result: PSA is regulated by both AR and GR, KLF9 by GR only, and PMEPA1 by AR only.
evaluation: Claims C77-C79 are established facts about gene regulation supported by citation to prior work (Arora et al., 2013). These provide the basis for interpreting the specificity experiments in Figure 3C.

result: The effect of 11β-HSD2 on tumor growth is specific to the context of AR antagonist therapy.
evaluation: Claim C80 is an inference supported by the observation that 11β-HSD2 expression affects tumor growth only in enzalutamide-treated xenografts (C26) but not untreated tumors (C27, Figure 4A-B). This context-specificity is important for understanding the therapeutic implications.
